title: Trace the path that is actually limiting checkout
description: Choose a symptom, trace the active request path, and inspect each component. The goal is to identify the evidence that supports the next change rather than choose a favorite optimization.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Starts checkout and experiences the end-to-end latency. A fast internal operation does not help if the complete request still waits elsewhere.

nodes.label: Checkout API
nodes.detail: Validates the request and coordinates the critical path. It should expose child timing, pool wait, and the remaining caller deadline.

nodes.label: Product cache
nodes.detail: Serves reconstructable product details within a stated freshness budget. A falling hit rate transfers work to the authoritative store.

nodes.label: Order database
nodes.detail: Commits orders and inventory decisions. Query plans, rows examined, lock wait, and pool wait identify whether this store limits the user path.

nodes.label: Fulfillment queue
nodes.detail: Buffers work after the order is durable. Queue age and rejected work matter more than queue depth alone when deciding whether customers will receive a confirmation on time.

nodes.label: Fulfillment worker
nodes.detail: Consumes post-checkout work. More workers help only when the queue is backed up and the worker's downstream dependencies still have headroom.

scenarios.label: Healthy baseline
scenarios.summary: Checkout p95 is 260 ms at 1,200 requests per second. The product cache is warm, database pool wait is near zero, and the fulfillment queue remains young.
scenarios.result: No intervention is justified yet. Preserve this workload mix and timing breakdown as the baseline for a later comparison.

scenarios.label: Cache-hit regression
scenarios.summary: A key-format deployment drops cache hits from 92% to 76%. Product reads now miss through to the database and its connection pool begins to wait.
scenarios.result: Inspect hit rate by key and cache state, then repair the key policy or coalesce duplicate misses. Scaling API workers would increase the database pressure.

scenarios.label: Slow order query
scenarios.summary: A new account-history query examines millions of rows to return 50. Database CPU is high, but the important evidence is a plan scan and rising query time on the checkout path.
scenarios.result: Run EXPLAIN with production-like parameters, inspect rows examined and buffers, then test a selective index or query rewrite. Add write-cost and rollback checks to the experiment.

scenarios.label: Fulfillment backlog
scenarios.summary: Checkout completes, but a promotion sends more fulfillment events than workers can drain. Queue age grows and delivery confirmations become late while the synchronous API remains healthy.
scenarios.result: Measure arrival rate, completion rate, queue age, and worker dependency headroom. Increase safe consumer capacity or throttle non-critical work; do not make checkout wait for fulfillment.
